content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors present FixEval - a large dataset of Python and Java programs with testcases and program evaluation verdicts that can be used in automatic bug fixing research. Authors have used FixEval for finetuning language models for automatic bug fixing task. Authors also present comparison of the results of the fine-tuned models and match-based metrics. Authors claim contributions of introducing FixEval dataset and comparison of state-of-the-art models on Fixeval.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- Introduces FixEval dataset that could be useful for conducting automatic bug fixing research
- Shows the necessity of execution-based evaluation of program repair results as well as the drawbacks of using just match-based metrics

Weaknesses:

- Claims to reflect real-world software applications, but actually uses short competition-based programs that differ a lot from large real-world applications
- It is rather obvious that execution-based metrics should win against naive match-based metrics. Authors do not compare execution-based metrics with something like symbolic evaluation
- Authors only compare fine-tuned models against Naive Copy baseline. It is not clear what benefit in terms of model finetuning the FixEval dataset provides.
- Not much in terms of novelty
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is mostly clearly written. Some suggestions for clarification below. 
In my opinion, there is not much novelty in the paper. The biggest contribution might be the construction of the dataset, but that's not novel.
Since authors open source the dataset and provide explanation of the fine-tuning of the models as well as explain the metrics used, the results should be reproducible.

------------------------------------------------------------
ICLR review form does not provide a section for comments/questions about the paper. I am going to post them here.

- What do authors mean by "Context-aware dataset"?
- "fails to reflect real-world software applications" – FixEval has the same issue.
- "these benchmarks lack relevance to real-world software" - FixEval has the same issue.
- What is the performance of the PLBART and CodeT5 on the problem set without finetuning?
- "two data points per problem from the test split, with a similar distribution of error verdicts," - please explain what you mean here.
- "we observe a marginal performance increase in our baseline models with verdict information as conditional input for Java programs. However, there was no such correlation for Python." - I guess verdict is a failure class and not "fail/not-fail". Please state this.
- "We compare match-based and execution-based evaluation metrics" – it is rather obvious that execution-based metrics will win against naïve match-based metrics. You need to have at least symbolic execution to evaluate program’s correctness without running it.
- It is interesting that Naïve Copy TCA is so high. I guess it makes sense, but it shows how hard baseline Naive Copy is if strict metrics are not used.
- "execution-based evaluation metric calculation requires substantial amount of time to evaluate a single program" – please state how much. 
- "To reduce computation complexity, we select two datapoints at random per problem from the test dataset." – please clarify. Is this 2 test cases??? Or two programs per problem?
content.summary_of_the_review: I think that the paper provides useful dataset, but overall, it is not novel enough for acceptance at ICLR.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces a new benchmark for code repair: a set of competitive programming submissions, both failed and successful. These submissions also come along with 1. a test suite that tests not only compilation but also runtime, memory, and functional correctness, 2. Many program submissions (in the millions), and 3. verdicts/extra metadata about the cause of the incorrect solutions.

This paper also analyzes the performance of a couple of baselines across a variety of settings, including both syntax-based performance and execution-based performance, as well as incorporating extra metadata about the verdicts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Overall, I think this is a worthy contribution as a code-repair dataset. It provides a combination of two qualities that I think are quite important in code datasets: 1. the ability to test for functional correctness, and 2. a large scale. Especially in code-repair, I've always been somewhat skeptical about whether match-based metrics test something meaningful. So, having hundreds of thousands of program pairs along with test cases for them is a significant step up.

The analysis and ablation into the "match-based metrics" vs. the "execution-based metrics" is also a valuable contribution.

In my opinion, the primary weakness of this paper is that much of the advantages of using a competitive programming derived dataset have already been established in the literature, such as in APPS (such as having unit tests and a large corpus of submissions). In addition, the actual benchmark itself does not demonstrate anything substantially surprising about the current SOTA models.

*However*, I do not think these are critical points for a dataset paper, especially one that provides a substantial leap forward to the "fundamentals" of a code benchmark (i.e. execution-based metrics and large scale). I would hope that this becomes one of the standard benchmarks for code repair.

Some nits:
1. Why not gather C++ submissions? C++ is the most popular language by some margin in competitive programming, and for a paper aiming to become a representative benchmark it seems like a somewhat strange omission.
2. 

> In AtCoder, contest problems come with a Task Label (e.g., A, B, C, D, E) and we conjecture that the label indicates the difficulty of the problem. 

I believe that this is typically fairly explicit on competitive programming websites.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The present work addresses the problem of evaluation of program fixes model by introducing FixEval, a new dataset that includes both Java, Python buggy code for code repair evaluation. The dataset it is created from two competitive programming submissions sources from AtCoder (Atcoder, 2020) and Aizu Online Judge (Aizu Online Judge, 2004), both datasets included in CodeNet (Puri et al, 2021) and CodeContests (Li et at, 2022), making them a standard benchmark code generation tasks.
FixEval is compared with existing benchmarks, in particular DeepFix, Review4Repair Bug2Fix, Github-Python, addressing the limitations of all of them (two programming languages instead of one, larger data test size) and the only that includes test cases.
The dataset is evaluated using CodeT5 and PLBART as baselines, in addition to a "copy" baseline (just copying the buggy input to the output), and evaluated in two set of metrics, MAtch-based metrics and execution based metrics
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The dataset introduced in this work is very much needed.
The models used as baselines were properly chosen.
Dataset source and curation seems reasonable.

Weaknesses

Execution based are not clear either.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a new benchmark called FixEval for evaluating a model's code repair capabilities. FixEval is derived from the CodeNet dataset and has test cases, so that one can evaluate execution-based correctness of the repaired code rather than just surface-level metrics like Bleu.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Code repair is an important task useful for automatic debugging and automatic grading and for giving feedback. Hence, having a large scale dataset for code repair tasks is useful. 

Previous works in other coding related tasks also figured out that metrics such as Bleu etc. do not really capture actual coding performance and hence, have proposed datasets with test cases to enable execution-based accuracy measurements. This paper does something similar but for code repair tasks (rather than code generation tasks). 

My main concern with the paper is that the contributions appear very thin. Especially, it is not clear to me how this dataset is different from the CodeNet dataset. Do the authors just reorganize the CodeNet dataset to make it a dataset for repair tasks or do they scrape additional data and perform some more cleaning up? I believe CodeNet dataset also has test cases to enable execution-based checking of generated programs. Are these test cases not sufficient that the authors collect more test cases? 

The evaluation is also very limited. The authors only evaluate CodeT5 and PLBART and do not include any of the latest/larger state-of-the-art large language models for Code such as Codex (through API access) or Incoder, GPT-J (which are publicly available).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is a bit ambiguous in several places. 
- The numbers in the introduction/table 1 about the statistics of the dataset don't seem to match with the numbers in the Section 3. 
- Why doesn't table 1 include datasets such as Defects4J and QuixBugs which are more closely related to the proposed dataset? 
- Does the training set also have test cases? If it does not, then how do you pick the accepted submission for the repair pair in the training dataset? 
- As mentioned above, the relationship to CodeNet dataset is not clear.
- What is the size of dataset before/after deduplication and filtering steps?
- Why keep only one submission per problem? Multiple submissions (even for the same problem) might represent different kinds of repair tasks. 
- What does "Example" mean in table 2? Is it the number of test cases or the number of code submissions?
- For finetuning and evaluation, what is the prompt? Does it include the problem description as well?


Additionally, do the authors measure the quality of their test cases. Prior works reported that most of these datasets do not have sufficient test cases which allow for false positives. Do the authors see something similar here?
content.summary_of_the_review: While the proposed dataset looks very promising, the writing needs improvement. In particular, the authors should carefully disentangle their contributions from the prior work (CodeNet dataset) and also evaluate on more recent models to establish strong baselines.
